CUSTODIAL ACCOUNT FOR A MINOR (UTMA) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Taylor Morgan

TRANSFER TO CUSTODIAN FOR A MINOR — DECLARATION
I, Jordan Alex Lee, transfer the property described below to Taylor Morgan, as custodian for Casey Rivera under the California Uniform Transfers to Minors Act. The property transferred is described as follows: $10,000 cash. This transfer is made pursuant to Probate Code Part 9 (commencing with Section 3900). This declaration is background information for use with the specific registration, delivery, or written-instrument steps that actually create custodial property under Probate Code § 3909 for property of this kind — for example, registering a security, brokerage account, or vehicle title, or recording an interest in real property, in the name of the custodian followed by the statutory custodial designation. Signing this declaration alone does not create custodial property; the applicable statutory method of transfer under § 3909 must actually be completed.

HOW A CUSTODIAL TRANSFER IS CREATED
California Probate Code § 3909(a) specifies that "[c]ustodial property is created and a transfer is made whenever any of the following occurs," and then lists distinct statutory methods keyed to the type of property involved. Securities are registered or delivered to the custodian; under § 3909(a)(2), "[m]oney is paid or delivered, or a security held in the name of a broker, financial institution, or its nominee is transferred, to a broker or financial institution for credit to an account in the name of the transferor, an adult other than the transferor, or a trust company, followed in substance by the words" of the statutory custodial designation. Life insurance and annuity interests, contract rights, and — under § 3909(a)(5) — real property ("[a]n interest in real property is recorded in the name of the transferor, an adult other than the transferor, or a trust company, followed in substance by the words" of that designation) each have their own listed method, and vehicle certificates of title have theirs. A residual category, § 3909(a)(7), covers "[a]n interest in any property not described in paragraphs (1) through (6)" and requires transfer "by a written instrument in substantially the form set forth in subdivision (b)." Across every one of these methods, the statutory designation itself takes the same recurring form: the recipient's name "followed in substance by the words" "as custodian for _____ (Name of Minor) _____ under the California Uniform Transfers to Minors Act."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Custodial property is created and a transfer is made whenever any of the following occurs:"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 3909 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 3909(a), (a)(2), (a)(5), (a)(7) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=3909.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Prob. Code § 3909), used as real evidence of California's specific statutory methods for creating custodial property under its version of the Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer, and other states' Uniform Transfers/Gifts to Minors Act statutes use similar but not identical mechanics. The clause draws on four subdivisions of a single code section — 3909(a) introductory language, (a)(2), (a)(5), and (a)(7) — as one source; no independent second source was located or is needed, since the statute itself is the primary and controlling authority for its own creation mechanics. This clause does not address which specific method applies to a given item of property, and does not itself create custodial property for anyone.

CUSTODIAN'S POWERS AND STANDARD OF CARE
California Probate Code § 3912(a) requires a custodian to "do all of the following: (1) Take control of custodial property. (2) Register or record title to custodial property if appropriate. (3) Collect, hold, manage, invest, and reinvest custodial property." In carrying out that management role, § 3912(b) sets the governing standard: "[i]n dealing with custodial property, a custodian shall observe the standard of care that would be observed by a prudent person dealing with property of another and is not limited by any other statute restricting investments by fiduciaries," subject to specified exceptions for an uncompensated custodian's liability for losses and for a custodian's discretion to retain property received from the transferor. Separately, Probate Code § 3913(a) grants broad authority over the property itself: "a custodian, acting in a custodial capacity, has all the rights, powers, and authority over custodial property that unmarried adult owners have over their own property, but a custodian may exercise those rights, powers, and authority in that capacity only."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In dealing with custodial property, a custodian shall observe the standard of care that would be observed by a prudent person dealing with property of another and is not limited by any other statute restricting investments by fiduciaries"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 3912 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 3912(a), (b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=3912.)
  "A custodian, acting in a custodial capacity, has all the rights, powers, and authority over custodial property that unmarried adult owners have over their own property, but a custodian may exercise those rights, powers, and authority in that capacity only."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 3913(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 3913(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=3913.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the management duties and "prudent person" standard California's Act actually imposes — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular custodianship, and not investment or fiduciary advice about how any specific custodian should manage any specific property. § 3912 and § 3913 are two different code sections addressing related but distinct points (day-to-day management duties and standard of care, versus the scope of the custodian's authority over the property), so they are treated here as two sources within the same statutory part rather than one; no source independent of the California Probate Code itself was located or is needed, since the statute is the primary authority for its own standard of care. This clause does not evaluate whether any particular custodian's conduct has met or fallen short of the prudent-person standard.

PERMITTED USES OF CUSTODIAL PROPERTY FOR THE MINOR
California Probate Code § 3914(a) states that "[a] custodian may deliver or pay to the minor or expend for the minor's benefit as much of the custodial property as the custodian considers advisable for the use and benefit of the minor, without court order and without regard to (1) the duty or ability of the custodian personally, or of any other person, to support the minor or (2) any other income or property of the minor which may be applicable or available for that purpose." Section 3914(c) clarifies that such a delivery, payment, or expenditure "is in addition to, not in substitution for, and does not affect, any obligation of a person to support the minor." Section 3914(d) also allows a transferor who is also the custodian to instead irrevocably elect a more restrictive standard, under which the custodian may not expend custodial property for the minor's use before the statutory transfer age except by court order on a showing that the expenditure is necessary for the minor's support, maintenance, or education.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A custodian may deliver or pay to the minor or expend for the minor’s benefit as much of the custodial property as the custodian considers advisable for the use and benefit of the minor, without court order and without regard to (1) the duty or ability of the custodian personally, or of any other person, to support the minor or (2) any other income or property of the minor which may be applicable or available for that purpose."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 3914(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 3914(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=3914.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's default standard for a custodian's discretionary spending on a minor's behalf, and of the separate, more restrictive standard a transferor-custodian may elect instead — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular custodianship, and not a statement about what any particular custodian should or must do with any particular minor's property. The clause draws on three subdivisions of a single code section, § 3914(a), (c), and (d), as one source; no independent second source was located or is needed. This clause does not determine whether any specific expenditure is or is not advisable for a specific minor's use and benefit.

TERMINATION OF THE CUSTODIANSHIP AND TRANSFER AGE
Under California Probate Code § 3920, a custodian "shall transfer in an appropriate manner the custodial property to the minor or to the minor's estate" upon the earliest of the minor's death or, absent a delayed transfer age, "[t]he minor's attainment of 18 years of age unless the time of transfer of the custodial property to the minor is delayed under Section 3920.5 to a time after the time the minor attains the age of 18 years." California's default transfer age under the Act is therefore 18, not a later age. Section 3920.5, however, lets a transferor specify a later transfer age in the instrument creating the transfer, within limits that vary by how the transfer was made: for a transfer by irrevocable gift under Section 3904, § 3920.5(e) allows delay only if the custodianship is to continue "until the time the minor attains a specified age, which time may not be later than the time the minor attains 21 years of age," while for a transfer made under a nomination or under a governing will or trust (Sections 3903 or 3905), § 3920.5(c) allows delay only up to "the time the minor attains 25 years of age."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The minor’s attainment of 18 years of age unless the time of transfer of the custodial property to the minor is delayed under Section 3920.5 to a time after the time the minor attains the age of 18 years."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 3920(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 3920(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=3920.)
  "The time for transfer to the minor of custodial property transferred by irrevocable gift under Section 3904 may be delayed under this section only if the transfer pursuant to Section 3909 provides in substance that the custodianship is to continue until the time the minor attains a specified age, which time may not be later than the time the minor attains 21 years of age."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 3920.5(e) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 3920.5(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=3920.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's Act sets a default transfer age of 18 — not 21 — with a transferor-selected later age (up to 21 or 25, depending on how the transfer was made) available only if specified in the transfer instrument under § 3920.5; this corrects a common assumption, since some other states' versions of the Act default to a later age. This is not a claim about which state's law governs a particular custodianship, nor a statement of what transfer age is or should be selected for any specific minor. § 3920 and § 3920.5 are two different code sections working together (the general termination rule and the age-delay mechanism), so they are treated as two sources within the same statutory part; no source independent of the California Probate Code itself was located or is needed. This clause does not address the delayed ages available for transfers made under Section 3906 (trustee transfers to a custodian) or under an irrevocable exercise of a power of appointment under Section 3904, which the statute also treats somewhat differently.

IRREVOCABILITY AND VESTED TITLE IN THE MINOR
California Probate Code § 3911(b) provides that "[a] transfer made pursuant to Section 3909 is irrevocable, and the custodial property is indefeasibly vested in the minor, but the custodian has all the rights, powers, duties, and authority provided in this part, and neither the minor nor the minor's legal representative has any right, power, duty, or authority with respect to the custodial property except as provided in this part." Legal title thus vests in the minor immediately and irrevocably once a transfer is made in the statutory manner, while control and management of the property remain with the custodian under the Act's own rules rather than with the minor.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A transfer made pursuant to Section 3909 is irrevocable, and the custodial property is indefeasibly vested in the minor, but the custodian has all the rights, powers, duties, and authority provided in this part, and neither the minor nor the minor’s legal representative has any right, power, duty, or authority with respect to the custodial property except as provided in this part."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 3911(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 3911(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=3911.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a properly completed transfer under California's Act is irrevocable and vests indefeasible legal title in the minor, subject to the custodian's statutory management powers — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular transfer, and not a statement about whether any specific transfer was, in fact, completed in the manner Section 3909 requires. Only Section 3911(b) is cited for this specific proposition; no independent second source was located or is needed, since the statute is the primary and controlling authority for the legal effect of its own transfers. This clause does not itself make, complete, or validate any transfer.

CUSTODIAN'S LIABILITY AND SUCCESSOR CUSTODIANS
California Probate Code § 3917(b) limits a custodian's personal liability, providing that "[a] custodian is not personally liable for either of the following: (1) On a contract properly entered into in the custodial capacity unless the custodian fails to reveal that capacity and to identify the custodianship in the contract. (2) For an obligation arising from control of custodial property or for a tort committed during the custodianship unless the custodian is personally at fault." Section 3918 separately addresses how a successor custodian can be put in place. Under § 3918(b), "[a] custodian at any time may designate a trust company or an adult other than a transferor under Section 3904 as successor custodian by executing and dating an instrument of designation before a subscribing witness other than the successor." If no successor was effectively designated and the custodian becomes ineligible, dies, or becomes incapacitated, § 3918(d) allows a minor who has attained 14 years of age to designate a successor, and otherwise provides that the minor's conservator becomes successor custodian, or that interested persons may petition the court to designate one. Section 3918(f) also lets specified persons, including the minor if 14 or older, "petition the court to remove the custodian for cause and to designate a successor custodian other than a transferor under Section 3904 or to require the custodian to give appropriate bond."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A custodian is not personally liable for either of the following: (1) On a contract properly entered into in the custodial capacity unless the custodian fails to reveal that capacity and to identify the custodianship in the contract. (2) For an obligation arising from control of custodial property or for a tort committed during the custodianship unless the custodian is personally at fault."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 3917(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 3917(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=3917.)
  "A custodian at any time may designate a trust company or an adult other than a transferor under Section 3904 as successor custodian by executing and dating an instrument of designation before a subscribing witness other than the successor."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 3918(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 3918(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=3918.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's specific rules limiting custodian liability absent personal fault and governing successor-custodian designation and court appointment — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular custodianship, and not an assessment of any specific custodian's liability or fitness to continue serving. § 3917 and § 3918 are two different code sections addressing distinct topics (liability, and succession), so they are treated as two sources within the same statutory part; the clause also draws on three subdivisions of § 3918 — (b), (d), and (f) — as parts of that single second source. No source independent of the California Probate Code itself was located or is needed. This clause does not address a custodian's compensation or bond requirements under Section 3915, which the statute treats separately.

SIGNATURE AND CERTIFICATION
Taylor Morgan, named above as custodian, acknowledges receipt of the property described above as custodian for Casey Rivera under the California Uniform Transfers to Minors Act, and certifies that this document will be held and administered together with the instrument, registration, or other transfer document that actually creates the custodial property under Probate Code § 3909. Signed in San Francisco, California on October 1, 2026.

_________________________
Jordan Alex Lee, Transferor

_________________________
Taylor Morgan, Custodian
